## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Graphs in Machine Learning
  Official title       Graphs in machine learning
  Instructors          D. CALANDRIELLO, M.VALKO, A.AZIZE (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 28 h (lectures 16 h, tutorials 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Machine Learning
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course description is written in English)
  Assessment           Short reports from the recitations; to be eligible for the resit (“rattrapage”), students must submit at least 2 homeworks on their deadlines and receive at least one third of the maximum homework score (master-mva.com); Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        Linear algebra and basic statistics; the other tools needed are covered in the lectures (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics or computer science who knows linear algebra and basic statistics, and who wants to learn from data that come with relations, or whose geometry is best captured by a neighbourhood graph.

**Empirical first**: in Zachary's karate club (34 members, 78 friendships), the sign of a single eigenvector of the graph Laplacian, computed from the friendships alone, predicts which side of the later split 33 of the 34 members joined ([ch. 1](#ch1)). On the handwritten digits of scikit-learn, with only 2 labelled images per class, propagating labels along a nearest-neighbour graph classifies 91.5 % of the 1777 other images, against 80.4 % for a logistic regression on the 20 labelled ones ([ch. 4](#ch4)).

This course explains both phenomena and builds on them. Graphs arise in two ways: as networks (social, biological, technological), and as neighbourhood graphs built from flat data such as images. The same object, the graph Laplacian, drives clustering, manifold learning, semi-supervised learning, online prediction and decision-making on graphs.

Every method comes with the question of scale: what it costs on a graph with millions of nodes, and which approximation keeps its guarantees.

The course shares tools with [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (the Laplacian pseudo-inverse is a kernel), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) and [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (bandits), and [Algorithms for Network Optimization and Management](../s2-network-optimization/index.html) (networks).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute and interpret the spectrum of the Laplacians of a graph: connected components, smooth functions, random walks and the Cheeger inequality.
-   Derive spectral clustering as a relaxation of a graph cut, implement it, and explain when it recovers the clusters.
-   Build a similarity graph from flat data, choose its parameters, and use its eigenvectors as a nonparametric basis and as a manifold embedding.
-   Solve semi-supervised problems with the harmonic function solution, its regularized variants and manifold regularization.
-   Prove a transductive generalization bound for graph-regularized learning through algorithmic stability.
-   Predict labels online on a graph with a perceptron, bound its mistakes, and run an online semi-supervised learner with bounded memory.
-   Scale graph methods with sparse iterative solvers, Nyström approximations and spectral sparsification, and bound the error each approximation adds.
-   Analyse bandit algorithms on graphs, from UCB1 to spectral bandits, and explain why the regret depends on an effective dimension rather than on the number of nodes.
-   Apply these tools to social networks (centrality, link prediction, influence), recommender systems and vision (face recognition, segmentation).

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com starts from the remark that graphs come in handy whenever we deal with relations between objects. The course, focused on learning, presents methods for two main sources of graphs in machine learning.

The first source is networks: social, biological or technological. The second is flat data, often from vision, where a graph serves as a useful nonparametric basis and an effective data representation for spectral clustering, manifold learning and semi-supervised learning.

The description also announces online decision-making on graphs, suitable for recommender systems or online advertising. It stresses that the scalability of every approach is always discussed, with how to address huge graphs in practice.

According to the description, the lectures show not only how but mostly why things work. Students learn the relevant parts of spectral graph theory, learning theory and bandit theory, the necessary mathematics, and concrete graph-based approaches to typical machine learning problems.

The practical sessions give hands-on experience on applications such as an online face recognizer, and with graph-processing tools such as GraphLab. The organisation announced is 7 lectures and 3 recitations (TP/TD) of 2 hours each, held online. The Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives only the type of assessment, with no programme of its own.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: linear algebra and basic statistics; the description says that the other tools needed are covered in the lectures. Ch. 0 collects them: the spectral theorem and Rayleigh quotients, Markov chains, and the concentration inequalities used by the learning-theory and bandit chapters.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (symmetric matrices, eigenvalues), [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (Markov chains, concentration) and [Scientific Python](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (NumPy, SciPy sparse matrices) cover the background.
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (risk, generalization bounds), [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (quadratic problems, strong convexity), [Geometric Data Analysis](../s1-geometric-data-analysis/index.html) (manifold learning), [ALTEGRAD](../s1-altegrad/index.html) (graph data and graph neural networks) and [Probabilistic Graphical Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (another meaning of “graph”).
-   **Related courses of semester 2** — [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (Laplacian kernels, Nyström), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) and [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (bandits), [Large Random Matrices](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html) (spectra of random graphs and kernel matrices), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) (graph cuts in vision), [Point Clouds and 3D Modelling](../s2-point-clouds-3d/index.html) (neighbourhood graphs on 3D points) and [Network Optimization](../s2-network-optimization/index.html).
-   **After the course** — the [research internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html); graph methods recur in [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html) (fairness on networks) and [Protein Science](../s2-protein-science/index.html) (interaction graphs).

### Course outline

-   **0. Review** — spectral theorem, Rayleigh quotients, Markov chains, Hoeffding and Azuma inequalities.
-   **1. Graphs, Laplacians and spectral graph theory** — where graphs come from, the three Laplacians, spectrum and connectivity, smoothness, random walks, the Cheeger inequality.
-   **2. Spectral clustering** — graph cuts, their spectral relaxations, the algorithms and why they work.
-   **3. Graphs from flat data and manifold learning** — similarity graphs, eigenvectors as a nonparametric basis, convergence to the Laplace–Beltrami operator, Laplacian eigenmaps.
-   **4. Semi-supervised learning on graphs** — the harmonic function solution, random walks and electric networks, soft constraints, manifold regularization.
-   **5. Learnability on graphs** — the transductive setting, algorithmic stability, concentration without replacement, a generalization bound.
-   **6. Adaptive online learning with graphs** — the graph perceptron and its mistake bound, the online harmonic solution on a quantized graph, the online face recognizer.
-   **7. Large graphs** — real-world graphs, iterative solvers, Nyström, spectral sparsification and its error analysis, distributed graph processing.
-   **8. Decision-making on graphs** — UCB1, linear bandits, spectral bandits and the effective dimension.
-   **9. Applications** — social networks, recommender systems and vision.
-   **10. Complements for self-study** — the hard side of the Cheeger inequality, diffusion maps, side observations and more graph bandits, influence maximization, graph neural networks.
-   **11. Research directions and open problems** — a self-study tour of current work.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1 if Rayleigh quotients or Markov chains feel distant; ch. 1–8 use them without warning.
-   Keep one small graph in mind throughout, the two triangles of Example 1.5: every definition of the course can be checked on it by hand.
-   After each session, do the exercises of its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (number of neighbours, bandwidth, regularization) to see its effect.
-   The code uses NumPy, SciPy (sparse matrices), scikit-learn and NetworkX, with synthetic data or data sets bundled with scikit-learn and NetworkX; every block runs in seconds on a laptop.
-   Each block sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to 1 before importing NumPy: at these problem sizes one BLAS thread is fastest, and some shared machines slow down badly with more.
-   The three recitations ask for a short report: write it as you go, with one figure and one paragraph of interpretation per question.
-   Start a project of the last section after session 6, once spectral and semi-supervised methods are in place.

## 0. Review: symmetric matrices, Markov chains and concentration {#ch0}

Graph methods compute with symmetric matrices, interpret them through random walks, and are analysed with concentration inequalities. This chapter collects the M1-level facts used later, with short proofs.

The [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and the [Probability and Statistics refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) cover the same ground at a slower pace.

### 0.1 Symmetric matrices and Rayleigh quotients

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Spectral theorem, Courant–Fischer and Ky Fan]{.tag} Let $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be symmetric. Then $S = U \Lambda U^\top$ with $U$ orthogonal and $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$, where $\lambda_1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$ are real.

The eigenvalues are minima of the Rayleigh quotient over nested subspaces:
$$
\lambda_k = \min_{\dim V = k}\ \max_{x \in V \setminus \{0\}} \frac{x^\top S x}{x^\top x},
\qquad
\lambda_k = \min_{x \perp u_1, \dots, u_{k-1}} \frac{x^\top S x}{x^\top x} .
$$

For $p \leq n$, the smallest trace over orthonormal families is the sum of the $p$ smallest eigenvalues, reached at $Y = (u_1, \dots, u_p)$:
$$
\min_{Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p},\ Y^\top Y = I_p} \mathrm{tr}\big(Y^\top S Y\big) = \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_p .
$$

::: proof
Write $x = U\alpha$. Then the Rayleigh quotient is a weighted mean of eigenvalues:
$$
\frac{x^\top S x}{x^\top x} = \frac{\sum_i \lambda_i \alpha_i^2}{\sum_i \alpha_i^2} .
$$

-   If $x \perp u_1, \dots, u_{k-1}$, then $\alpha_1 = \dots = \alpha_{k-1} = 0$ and the mean is at least $\lambda_k$, with equality at $x = u_k$.
-   Any $V$ of dimension $k$ meets $\mathrm{span}(u_k, \dots, u_n)$ in a non-zero vector, whose quotient is at least $\lambda_k$; the choice $V = \mathrm{span}(u_1, \dots, u_k)$ gives exactly $\lambda_k$.
-   For the trace, $\mathrm{tr}(Y^\top S Y) = \sum_i \lambda_i c_i$ with $c_i = \|Y^\top u_i\|^2 \in [0, 1]$ and $\sum_i c_i = p$. A linear function of $c$ on this set is smallest when the $p$ smallest $\lambda_i$ get weight 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Loewner order and pseudo-inverse]{.tag} A symmetric matrix $S$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $S \succeq 0$, when $x^\top S x \geq 0$ for all $x$, that is when all its eigenvalues are non-negative. We write $A \preceq B$ when $B - A \succeq 0$.

The **Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse** of $S = \sum_i \lambda_i u_i u_i^\top$ inverts the non-zero eigenvalues and keeps the zero ones:
$$
S^{+} = \sum_{i:\ \lambda_i \neq 0} \lambda_i^{-1}\, u_i u_i^\top .
$$
:::

If $\alpha I \preceq S \preceq \beta I$ with $\alpha > 0$, then $\|S^{-1}\| \leq 1/\alpha$, and the condition number of $S$ is at most $\beta / \alpha$. Ch. 5–7 use these two facts constantly.

### 0.2 Markov chains on a finite set

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Stationary and reversible chains]{.tag} A **transition matrix** $P$ on a finite set has non-negative entries and rows summing to 1. A probability vector $\pi$ is **stationary** when $\pi^\top P = \pi^\top$. The chain is **reversible** with respect to $\pi$ when
$$
\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji} \qquad \text{for all } i, j .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Spectrum of a reversible chain]{.tag} If $P$ is reversible with respect to $\pi > 0$, then $\Pi^{1/2} P\, \Pi^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, where $\Pi = \mathrm{diag}(\pi)$. Hence $P$ has real eigenvalues, all in $[-1, 1]$, and a basis of eigenvectors.

::: proof
The $(i, j)$ entry of $\Pi^{1/2} P\, \Pi^{-1/2}$ is $\sqrt{\pi_i}\, P_{ij} / \sqrt{\pi_j}$. Reversibility makes it equal to $\sqrt{\pi_j}\, P_{ji} / \sqrt{\pi_i}$, the $(j, i)$ entry.

The matrix is similar to $P$, so they share eigenvalues. Since the rows of $P$ are probability vectors, $\|Px\|_\infty \leq \|x\|_\infty$, so every eigenvalue has modulus at most 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A random walk on a graph is reversible (ch. 1.5). This is why its analysis reduces to the spectrum of a symmetric matrix.

### 0.3 Concentration inequalities

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Hoeffding and Azuma–Hoeffding]{.tag} Let $M_0, M_1, \dots, M_m$ be a martingale whose increments $D_k = M_k - M_{k-1}$ lie, given the past, in an interval of length $c_k$. Then for $t > 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\big(M_m - M_0 \geq t\big) \leq \exp\Big( - \frac{2 t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^m c_k^2} \Big) .
$$

For independent variables $X_k \in [a_k, b_k]$ and $M_m = \sum_k (X_k - \mathbb{E} X_k)$, this is Hoeffding's inequality with $c_k = b_k - a_k$.
::::

::: proof
*Hoeffding's lemma*: a centred variable $D \in [a, a + c]$ satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}\, e^{sD} \leq e^{s^2 c^2 / 8} .
$$

Applied conditionally on the past, and by induction on $m$, it gives
$$
\mathbb{E}\, e^{s(M_m - M_0)} \leq \exp\Big(\frac{s^2}{8} \sum_k c_k^2\Big) .
$$

Markov's inequality on $e^{s(M_m - M_0)}$ then gives the bound $\exp(-st + s^2 \sum_k c_k^2 / 8)$. The choice $s = 4t / \sum_k c_k^2$ concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The **method of bounded differences** applies this to the Doob martingale $M_k = \mathbb{E}[h \mid Z_1, \dots, Z_k]$ of a function $h$ of independent variables. If changing one variable moves $h$ by at most $c_k$, the increments have ranges at most $c_k$: this is McDiarmid's inequality. Ch. 5 adapts the argument to sampling without replacement.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are minima of Rayleigh quotients; the sum of the $p$ smallest is the minimal trace over orthonormal $p$-frames.
-   A reversible Markov chain is a symmetric matrix in disguise: real spectrum in $[-1, 1]$.
-   Martingales with bounded increments concentrate like sums of independent bounded variables.
:::

## 1. Graphs, Laplacians and spectral graph theory {#ch1}

A graph encodes which objects are related and how strongly. This chapter introduces the matrix that turns the graph into a tool for learning, the Laplacian, and reads the structure of the graph from its spectrum.

### 1.1 Where graphs come from

Graphs reach machine learning by two routes.

-   **Networks** are given by the application: people and friendships, proteins and their interactions, web pages and hyperlinks, users and the items they bought.
-   **Similarity graphs** are built from flat data: each data point becomes a node, and close points are joined by an edge weighted by their similarity (ch. 3).

In both cases the graph carries an assumption: related nodes tend to share labels or values. The course turns this assumption into algorithms and guarantees.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Weighted graph, degree, volume]{.tag} A **weighted undirected graph** on the nodes $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is given by a symmetric matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with $w_{ij} \geq 0$ and $w_{ii} = 0$. There is an edge $i \sim j$ when $w_{ij} > 0$.

The **degree** of node $i$ and the **volume** of a set $A \subseteq V$ are
$$
d_i = \sum_{j} w_{ij}, \qquad \mathrm{vol}(A) = \sum_{i \in A} d_i .
$$

We write $D = \mathrm{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_n)$ and assume $d_i > 0$ (no isolated node). An unweighted graph has $w_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$.
:::

### 1.2 The graph Laplacians

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Three Laplacians]{.tag} The **unnormalized Laplacian**, the **symmetric normalized Laplacian** and the **random-walk Laplacian** are
$$
L = D - W, \qquad L_{\mathrm{sym}} = D^{-1/2} L\, D^{-1/2} = I - D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}, \qquad L_{\mathrm{rw}} = D^{-1} L = I - D^{-1} W .
$$
:::

A vector $f \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a function on the nodes, and $(Lf)_i = \sum_j w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)$ compares the value at $i$ with its neighbours. The quadratic form of $L$ measures how much $f$ varies along the edges.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — The Laplacian quadratic form]{.tag} For every $f \in \mathbb{R}^n$,

::: key
[Key formula — smoothness of a function on a graph]{.tag}
$$
f^\top L f = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij}\, (f_i - f_j)^2 \ \geq\ 0 .
$$
:::

Consequently $L$ and $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ are symmetric positive semidefinite, and $L \mathbf{1} = 0$.

Moreover $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$ has the same eigenvalues as $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$: each eigenvector $v$ of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ gives the eigenvector $D^{-1/2} v$ of $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$.

::: proof
-   Expand the right-hand side:
    $$
    \frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij} w_{ij}(f_i^2 + f_j^2) - \sum_{ij} w_{ij} f_i f_j .
    $$
-   The first sum equals $\sum_i d_i f_i^2 = f^\top D f$ by symmetry of $W$, and the second is $f^\top W f$.
-   For $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$, apply the identity to $g = D^{-1/2} f$: $f^\top L_{\mathrm{sym}} f = g^\top L g \geq 0$.
-   Finally, $L_{\mathrm{sym}} v = \lambda v$ is equivalent to $D^{-1} L (D^{-1/2} v) = \lambda D^{-1/2} v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The eigenvalue problem of $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$ is the generalized problem $L u = \lambda D u$. The three Laplacians differ in how they weigh the nodes; ch. 2 and ch. 3 explain when the difference matters.

### 1.3 Spectrum and connectivity

We order the eigenvalues of $L$ as $0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$, with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1, \dots, u_n$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Zero eigenvalues count the components]{.tag} The multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 of $L$ equals the number $k$ of connected components $A_1, \dots, A_k$ of the graph. Its eigenspace is spanned by the indicator vectors $\mathbf{1}_{A_1}, \dots, \mathbf{1}_{A_k}$.

The same holds for $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$. For $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ the eigenspace is spanned by the vectors $D^{1/2} \mathbf{1}_{A_j}$.

::: proof
If $Lf = 0$, then $f^\top L f = 0$, so $f_i = f_j$ whenever $w_{ij} > 0$ by Proposition 1.3. Along a path the value cannot change, so $f$ is constant on each component.

Conversely each indicator $\mathbf{1}_{A_j}$ satisfies $L \mathbf{1}_{A_j} = 0$, since no edge leaves $A_j$. The indicators are orthogonal, so the kernel has dimension exactly $k$. The statements for $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ follow from Proposition 1.3. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

So $\lambda_2 > 0$ if and only if the graph is connected. Fiedler (1973) called $\lambda_2$ the **algebraic connectivity**, and $u_2$ is the **Fiedler vector**.

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — Two triangles joined by a bridge]{.tag} Take the nodes $0, 1, 2$ forming a triangle, the nodes $3, 4, 5$ forming another, and the bridge $2 \sim 3$, all weights 1.

-   Degrees: $d = (2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2)$, with $7$ edges and total volume $14$.
-   The spectrum of $L$ is
    $$
    0,\quad \tfrac{5 - \sqrt{17}}{2} \approx 0.438,\quad 3,\quad 3,\quad 3,\quad \tfrac{5 + \sqrt{17}}{2} \approx 4.562 .
    $$
-   The Fiedler vector is $u_2 \approx (-0.465, -0.465, -0.261, 0.261, 0.465, 0.465)$. Its sign separates the two triangles, and its smallest values in modulus sit at the ends of the bridge.
-   The spectrum of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is $0, 0.205, 1.167, 1.5, 1.5, 1.629$.

Removing the bridge gives two components and a second zero eigenvalue: $\lambda_2 = 0.438$ is small because the graph is *almost* disconnected.
:::

Two more spectra are worth remembering. The complete graph on $n$ nodes has eigenvalues $0$ and $n$, the latter with multiplicity $n - 1$.

The path on $n$ nodes has eigenvalues $2 - 2\cos(\pi k / n)$ for $k = 0, \dots, n - 1$. Its $\lambda_2$ is of order $\pi^2 / n^2$: long paths are poorly connected.

### 1.4 Smooth functions and the graph Fourier basis

Expand a function on the nodes in the eigenbasis, $f = \sum_i \alpha_i u_i$ with $\alpha_i = u_i^\top f$. By Proposition 1.3 and orthonormality,
$$
f^\top L f = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\, \alpha_i^2 .
$$

The eigenvectors with small eigenvalues vary slowly along the edges, and those with large eigenvalues oscillate. By Theorem 0.1, $u_k$ is the smoothest unit function orthogonal to $u_1, \dots, u_{k-1}$.

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Graph Fourier transform]{.tag} The **graph Fourier transform** of $f$ is the vector $\hat f = U^\top f$ of its coefficients in the eigenbasis of $L$. The eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ plays the role of a squared frequency. A **low-pass filter** keeps the coefficients of small $\lambda_i$:
$$
h(L)\, f = \sum_{i=1}^n h(\lambda_i)\, \alpha_i\, u_i, \qquad h \text{ decreasing}.
$$
:::

On a cycle, the eigenvectors are sines and cosines, and the transform is the discrete Fourier transform. On a general graph there is no translation, but smoothness still has a meaning: the energy $f^\top L f$. Ch. 3 uses the first eigenvectors as a basis for regression, and ch. 4 and ch. 8 use $f^\top L f$ as a regularizer.

### 1.5 Random walks and the Cheeger inequality

The **random walk** on the graph moves from $i$ to $j$ with probability $P_{ij} = w_{ij} / d_i$, so $P = D^{-1} W$ and $L_{\mathrm{rw}} = I - P$.

The distribution $\pi_i = d_i / \mathrm{vol}(V)$ is stationary, and the walk is reversible: $\pi_i P_{ij} = w_{ij} / \mathrm{vol}(V)$ is symmetric in $i, j$.

By Proposition 0.4 the spectrum of $P$ is real: it consists of the values $1 - \lambda$, for the eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$.

On a connected, non-bipartite graph the walk converges to $\pi$. A small $\lambda_2(L_{\mathrm{sym}})$ means a slow walk, trapped on one side of a bottleneck; the Cheeger inequality makes this exact.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Cheeger inequality]{.tag} The **conductance** of a set $S$ and of the graph are
$$
\phi(S) = \frac{\mathrm{cut}(S, \bar S)}{\min\big(\mathrm{vol}(S), \mathrm{vol}(\bar S)\big)}, \qquad \phi(G) = \min_{\emptyset \neq S \subsetneq V} \phi(S),
$$
where $\mathrm{cut}(S, \bar S) = \sum_{i \in S, j \notin S} w_{ij}$ is the weight of the edges leaving $S$.

Let $\lambda_2$ be the second smallest eigenvalue of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ of a connected graph. Then
$$
\frac{\lambda_2}{2} \ \leq\ \phi(G) \ \leq\ \sqrt{2 \lambda_2} .
$$

::: proof
*Left inequality.* By Theorem 0.1 applied to $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and the substitution $g = D^{1/2} f$,
$$
\lambda_2 = \min_{f \neq 0,\ \sum_i d_i f_i = 0} \frac{f^\top L f}{f^\top D f} .
$$

Take any $S$, write $a = 1/\mathrm{vol}(S)$ and $b = 1/\mathrm{vol}(\bar S)$, and take the test function
$$
f = a\, \mathbf{1}_S - b\, \mathbf{1}_{\bar S}, \qquad \text{which satisfies} \quad \sum_i d_i f_i = 1 - 1 = 0 .
$$

-   Only the edges of the cut contribute to $f^\top L f$, each with the squared jump $(a + b)^2$.
-   The denominator is $f^\top D f = a + b$, since $a^2\, \mathrm{vol}(S) = a$ and $b^2\, \mathrm{vol}(\bar S) = b$.
-   The quotient is therefore $(a + b)\, \mathrm{cut}(S, \bar S)$, at most $2 \max(a, b)\, \mathrm{cut}(S, \bar S) = 2\phi(S)$.

So $\lambda_2 \leq 2\phi(S)$ for every $S$, which is the left inequality.

*Right inequality.* It is proved by a sweep: order the nodes by the values of $D^{-1/2} v_2$ and take the best of the $n - 1$ threshold sets. A co-area argument and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality show that this set has conductance at most $\sqrt{2\lambda_2}$; ch. 10.1 gives the proof. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On the two triangles of Example 1.5, the cut at the bridge has conductance $1/7 \approx 0.143$. Cheeger's bounds are $0.102 \leq \phi(G) \leq 0.640$: the lower bound is close, the upper one is loose, as is typical.

The code computes the Fiedler vector of Zachary's karate club, a friendship network of 34 members recorded before the club split in two (Zachary, 1977), shipped with NetworkX.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()                       # 34 members, 78 friendships
L = nx.laplacian_matrix(G).toarray().astype(float)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(L)
print("n =", G.number_of_nodes(), " edges =", G.number_of_edges())
print("lambda_2 =", round(vals[1], 4))
side = np.array([G.nodes[v]["club"] == "Officer" for v in G])   # the side joined after the split
pred = vecs[:, 1] > 0                            # sign of the Fiedler vector
agree = max((pred == side).sum(), (pred != side).sum())
print(f"the sign of u_2 matches the split for {agree} of 34 members")
```

It prints $\lambda_2 = 1.1871$ and 33 of 34: friendships alone predict the split, without any label. This is the starting point of spectral clustering.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   $L = D - W$, $L_{\mathrm{sym}} = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}$, $L_{\mathrm{rw}} = D^{-1} L$; all are positive semidefinite and $f^\top L f = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} w_{ij} (f_i - f_j)^2$.
-   The multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 is the number of connected components; a small $\lambda_2$ signals a bottleneck.
-   Eigenvectors of $L$ form a Fourier basis ordered by smoothness.
-   The random walk $P = D^{-1} W$ is reversible with stationary law $d / \mathrm{vol}(V)$, and Cheeger: $\lambda_2 / 2 \leq \phi(G) \leq \sqrt{2 \lambda_2}$.
:::

## 2. Spectral clustering {#ch2}

Clustering a graph means cutting few edges while keeping the pieces large. The exact problem is NP-hard; spectral clustering solves a relaxation with eigenvectors of a Laplacian. This chapter derives the relaxation, states the algorithms, and explains when they recover the clusters.

### 2.1 Graph cuts

For disjoint sets $A, B \subseteq V$ write $\mathrm{cut}(A, B) = \sum_{i \in A, j \in B} w_{ij}$, and let $|A|$ be the number of nodes of $A$.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Balanced cuts]{.tag} For a partition $A_1, \dots, A_k$ of $V$, the **ratio cut** and the **normalized cut** are
$$
\mathrm{RatioCut}(A_1, \dots, A_k) = \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{\mathrm{cut}(A_j, \bar A_j)}{|A_j|}, \qquad \mathrm{NCut}(A_1, \dots, A_k) = \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{\mathrm{cut}(A_j, \bar A_j)}{\mathrm{vol}(A_j)} .
$$
:::

The plain minimum cut is easy to compute but useless for clustering: it usually isolates a single weakly connected node. Dividing by the size or the volume penalizes small pieces. The price is complexity: minimizing these balanced cuts is NP-hard (Wagner and Wagner, 1993).

### 2.2 Spectral relaxations

The key observation is that a cut is a Laplacian quadratic form evaluated at a well-chosen vector.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Ratio cut as a Rayleigh quotient]{.tag} For a partition $(A, \bar A)$, define $f \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by
$$
f_i = \sqrt{|\bar A| / |A|} \ \text{ if } i \in A, \qquad f_i = -\sqrt{|A| / |\bar A|} \ \text{ if } i \in \bar A .
$$
Then $f \perp \mathbf{1}$, $\|f\|^2 = n$ and $f^\top L f = n\, \mathrm{RatioCut}(A, \bar A)$.

::: proof
-   Only edges between $A$ and $\bar A$ contribute to $f^\top L f$ (Proposition 1.3).
-   Each contributes its weight times the squared jump, $|\bar A|/|A| + |A|/|\bar A| + 2 = n/|A| + n/|\bar A|$.
-   The sum is therefore
    $$
    \mathrm{cut}(A, \bar A)\, \Big(\frac{n}{|A|} + \frac{n}{|\bar A|}\Big) = n\,\mathrm{RatioCut}(A, \bar A) .
    $$
-   The other two identities are direct: $\sum_i f_i = \sqrt{|A||\bar A|} - \sqrt{|A||\bar A|} = 0$ and $\|f\|^2 = |\bar A| + |A|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Minimizing the ratio cut is thus minimizing $f^\top L f$ over vectors of this two-valued form, subject to $f \perp \mathbf{1}$ and $\|f\|^2 = n$.

**Relaxing** the two-valued constraint to any real $f$ gives, by Theorem 0.1, the Fiedler vector $u_2$. One then rounds $u_2$ back to a partition, by its sign or by $k$-means on its values.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Normalized cut and the generalized problem]{.tag} With $f_i = \sqrt{\mathrm{vol}(\bar A) / \mathrm{vol}(A)}$ on $A$ and $f_i = -\sqrt{\mathrm{vol}(A) / \mathrm{vol}(\bar A)}$ on $\bar A$, one has
$$
(Df)^\top \mathbf{1} = 0, \qquad f^\top D f = \mathrm{vol}(V), \qquad f^\top L f = \mathrm{vol}(V)\ \mathrm{NCut}(A, \bar A) .
$$
The relaxation is the second eigenvector of the generalized problem $L u = \lambda D u$, that is of $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$ (Shi and Malik, 2000).

For $k$ clusters, let $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ have entries $H_{ij} = |A_j|^{-1/2}\, \mathbb{1}[i \in A_j]$. Then $H^\top H = I_k$ and
$$
\mathrm{RatioCut}(A_1, \dots, A_k) = \mathrm{tr}\big(H^\top L H\big) .
$$
Relaxing $H$ to any orthonormal $n \times k$ matrix gives, by the Ky Fan part of Theorem 0.1, the first $k$ eigenvectors of $L$. The same holds for the normalized cut with $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$.
::::

The proof of the two-set identities is that of Proposition 2.2 with volumes in place of sizes. For the trace, $(H^\top L H)_{jj} = \mathrm{cut}(A_j, \bar A_j) / |A_j|$ by the same computation applied to one indicator.

### 2.3 The algorithms

::: thm
[Algorithm 2.4 — Spectral clustering]{.tag} Input: a similarity matrix $W$ and a number of clusters $k$.

1.  Compute the first $k$ eigenvectors $u_1, \dots, u_k$ of a Laplacian, and stack them as the columns of $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$:
    -   *unnormalized*: eigenvectors of $L$;
    -   *Shi–Malik*: generalized eigenvectors $L u = \lambda D u$, that is of $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$;
    -   *Ng–Jordan–Weiss*: eigenvectors of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$, then each row of $U$ normalized to norm 1.
2.  Treat row $i$ of $U$ as a point $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$, the **spectral embedding** of node $i$.
3.  Cluster $y_1, \dots, y_n$ with $k$-means, and give node $i$ the cluster of $y_i$.
:::

The row normalization of Ng, Jordan and Weiss (2002) compensates for the factor $D^{1/2}$ in the eigenvectors of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ (Proposition 1.4), which would otherwise pull low-degree nodes towards the origin.

*Cost.* A dense eigendecomposition costs $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n^2)$ memory. On a sparse graph with $m$ edges, a Lanczos method computes the $k$ smallest eigenvectors in roughly $O(k\, m)$ operations per iteration; ch. 7 returns to this.

### 2.4 Why it works

Start from the ideal case, then perturb it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — The ideal case]{.tag} Suppose the graph has exactly $k$ connected components $A_1, \dots, A_k$, and let $U$ be any orthonormal basis of the kernel of $L$.

Then the rows $y_i$ of $U$ take exactly $k$ distinct values, one per component, and these values are pairwise orthogonal. Hence $k$-means recovers the components exactly.

::: proof
By Proposition 1.4, the kernel is spanned by the orthonormal columns of $H$, where $H_{ij} = |A_j|^{-1/2}\mathbb{1}[i \in A_j]$. So $U = H O$ for an orthogonal $k \times k$ matrix $O$.

When $i \in A_j$, row $i$ of $U$ is row $j$ of $O$ divided by $\sqrt{|A_j|}$, and the rows of an orthogonal matrix are orthonormal. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A real graph has a few edges between clusters. Write $L = \tilde L + E$, where $\tilde L$ is the Laplacian without the between-cluster edges. The question is how far the eigenvectors of $L$ move from those of $\tilde L$.

::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Davis–Kahan, in the form of Yu, Wang and Samworth (2015)]{.tag} Let $L$ and $\tilde L$ be symmetric, with bottom-$k$ eigenvectors $U$ and $\tilde U$.

Assume that the eigengap of $\tilde L$ is positive: $\tilde\lambda_{k+1} > \tilde\lambda_k$.

Then there is an orthogonal $k \times k$ matrix $O$ with
$$
\big\| U O - \tilde U \big\|_F \ \leq\ \frac{2^{3/2} \sqrt{k}\ \|L - \tilde L\|}{\tilde\lambda_{k+1} - \tilde\lambda_k} .
$$
:::

The proof is in Davis and Kahan (1970) and Yu, Wang and Samworth (2015). For spectral clustering it gives three messages.

-   The embedding is stable when the between-cluster weight $\|E\|$ is small compared with the gap $\tilde\lambda_{k+1}$, that is when each cluster is itself well connected (Cheeger, Theorem 1.7).
-   Rows that move by less than half the distance between ideal rows stay in the right cluster. Lei and Rinaldo (2015) turn this into a bound on the number of misclustered nodes in the stochastic block model.
-   The **eigengap heuristic** chooses $k$ where $\lambda_{k+1} - \lambda_k$ is large.

Which Laplacian? As the sample grows, normalized spectral clustering converges under mild conditions, while the unnormalized version can fail to (von Luxburg, Belkin and Bousquet, 2008). The safe default is $L_{\mathrm{rw}}$ or $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$.

### 2.5 An example where $k$-means fails

Two concentric noisy circles are not linearly separable, and no partition into two convex cells can split them. A 10-nearest-neighbour graph connects points along each circle and rarely across.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import laplacian
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

X, y = make_circles(n_samples=600, factor=0.4, noise=0.08, random_state=0)
W = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=10, include_self=False)
W = 0.5 * (W + W.T)                                   # symmetric 10-NN graph
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(laplacian(W, normed=True).toarray())
print("smallest eigenvalues of L_sym:", np.round(vals[:4], 4))

U = vecs[:, :2]                                       # Ng-Jordan-Weiss: k = 2 eigenvectors
U = U / np.linalg.norm(U, axis=1, keepdims=True)      # normalize the rows
spectral = KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(U)
direct = KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(X)
print("adjusted Rand index, spectral clustering:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y, spectral), 3))
print("adjusted Rand index, k-means on X       :", round(adjusted_rand_score(y, direct), 3))
```

The graph is connected, with smallest eigenvalues $0$, $0.0003$, $0.003$ and $0.0034$. The second is ten times smaller than the third: the eigengap heuristic says $k = 2$.

Spectral clustering recovers the two circles exactly (adjusted Rand index 1.0), while $k$-means on the raw coordinates is at chance level (index $-0.002$).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Ratio and normalized cuts are Laplacian quadratic forms of two-valued vectors; relaxing to real vectors gives eigenvectors.
-   Spectral clustering = first $k$ eigenvectors of a Laplacian, rows as points, then $k$-means.
-   It is exact when the clusters are components, and stable when the between-cluster weight is small compared with the eigengap (Davis–Kahan).
-   Prefer the normalized Laplacians: they are consistent as the sample grows.
:::

## 3. Graphs from flat data and manifold learning {#ch3}

Most data come as vectors without relations. A neighbourhood graph supplies the relations, and its Laplacian then serves as a nonparametric basis, as a description of the geometry of the data, and as a regularizer. This chapter builds the graph, says what its Laplacian converges to, and uses its eigenvectors as coordinates.

### 3.1 Similarity graphs

Let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be data points, and $s(x, x') = \exp(-\|x - x'\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)$ a Gaussian similarity of bandwidth $\sigma$.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Three similarity graphs]{.tag}

-   **$\varepsilon$-graph**: $i \sim j$ when $\|x_i - x_j\| \leq \varepsilon$, usually unweighted.
-   **$k$-nearest-neighbour graph**: $i \sim j$ when one of the two points is among the $k$ nearest neighbours of the other (symmetric graph). The **mutual** graph requires both. Edges are unweighted or weighted by the similarity.
-   **Fully connected graph**: $w_{ij} = s(x_i, x_j)$ for all $i \neq j$.
:::

The choice matters more than the choice of Laplacian. Three rules of thumb summarize experience and the theory below.

-   **Connectivity first.** Spectral methods cannot transmit information between components. For $n$ uniform points in $[0, 1]^p$, the $\varepsilon$-graph becomes connected when $n\varepsilon^p$ is of order $\log n$ (Penrose, 2003).

    For $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs, $k$ of order $\log n$ plays the same role.
-   **Sparsity.** $k$-NN and $\varepsilon$-graphs have $O(nk)$ edges; the fully connected graph has $n^2/2$, which is prohibitive beyond a few thousand points without the approximations of ch. 7.
-   **Adaptivity.** The $k$-NN graph adapts to the local density: it connects points in sparse regions as well as in dense ones. A single $\varepsilon$ cannot do both. A common bandwidth choice is the median distance to the $k$-th neighbour.

### 3.2 Graphs as a nonparametric basis

The eigenvectors $u_1, u_2, \dots$ of $L$ are ordered by smoothness on the graph (ch. 1.4). They play the role of a Fourier basis adapted to the data: no parametric model, only the graph.

Suppose noisy values $y = f + \epsilon$ are observed at the nodes, with independent centred noise of variance $\sigma^2$. The **projection estimator** keeps the first $m$ coefficients:
$$
\hat f_m = U_m U_m^\top y, \qquad U_m = (u_1, \dots, u_m) .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Bias and variance of the projection estimator]{.tag} With $\lambda_1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$ the eigenvalues of $L$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|\hat f_m - f\|^2 = \big\|(I - U_m U_m^\top) f\big\|^2 + m\, \sigma^2 \ \leq\ \frac{f^\top L f}{\lambda_{m+1}} + m\, \sigma^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write $P = U_m U_m^\top$, an orthogonal projection of rank $m$. Then $\hat f_m - f = -(I - P) f + P\epsilon$.

-   The cross term has zero mean, since $\mathbb{E}\,\epsilon = 0$.
-   The variance term is $\mathbb{E}\|P\epsilon\|^2 = m \sigma^2$, since $P$ has trace $m$.
-   With $\alpha_i = u_i^\top f$, the bias term is
    $$
    \sum_{i > m} \alpha_i^2 \leq \frac{1}{\lambda_{m+1}} \sum_{i > m} \lambda_i \alpha_i^2 \leq \frac{f^\top L f}{\lambda_{m+1}} .
    $$
    [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The trade-off is the classical one: more basis vectors reduce the bias, at a cost $\sigma^2$ each. A function that is smooth on the graph, with small $f^\top L f$, is learned with few eigenvectors.

### 3.3 What the graph Laplacian converges to

As the sample grows and the bandwidth shrinks, the graph Laplacian approaches a differential operator on the space the data live in. The one-dimensional computation shows the mechanism.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Pointwise limit in dimension one]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with a smooth density $p$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $k$ be a symmetric kernel with $\int k = 1$ and $\mu_2 = \int u^2 k(u)\, du$, and set $k_h(z) = h^{-1} k(z / h)$. For a smooth $f$, define
$$
(L_{n,h} f)(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^n k_h(x - X_j)\, \big( f(x) - f(X_j) \big) .
$$
Then, as $h \to 0$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\,(L_{n,h} f)(x) = -\frac{\mu_2 h^2}{2}\, \big( p f'' + 2 p' f' \big)(x) + O(h^3) .
$$

::: proof
Substitute $y = x + hu$ in the expectation $\int k_h(x - y)(f(x) - f(y))\, p(y)\, dy$:
$$
\int k(u)\, \big(f(x) - f(x + hu)\big)\, p(x + hu)\, du .
$$

-   Taylor: $f(x) - f(x + hu) = -hu f' - \tfrac{1}{2} h^2 u^2 f'' + O(h^3)$ and $p(x + hu) = p + hu\, p' + O(h^2)$.
-   The product is
    $$
    -hu\, f' p - h^2 u^2 \Big(\tfrac{1}{2} f'' p + f' p'\Big) + O(h^3) .
    $$
-   Integrating against the symmetric $k$ kills the odd term and leaves $-\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_2 h^2 (p f'' + 2 p' f')$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The variance of $L_{n,h} f(x)$ is of order $h / n$, so the rescaled operator $2 L_{n,h} / (\mu_2 h^2)$ converges in probability when $h \to 0$ and $n h^3 \to \infty$.

The general result, for data sampled on a $d$-dimensional submanifold $\mathcal{M}$ with density $p$, is due to Belkin and Niyogi (2008) and Hein, Audibert and von Luxburg (2007). Up to constants, the unnormalized graph Laplacian converges to the weighted Laplace–Beltrami operator
$$
f \ \longmapsto\ -\, p\, \Big( \Delta_{\mathcal{M}} f + 2 \big\langle \nabla \log p,\ \nabla f \big\rangle \Big),
$$
when $h \to 0$ and $n h^{d+2} / \log n \to \infty$. The random-walk Laplacian divides by the degree, which approximates $p$, and removes the outer factor.

Two consequences matter in practice. The graph sees the intrinsic dimension $d$ of the data, not the ambient dimension $p$. And the density enters the limit: graph methods favour functions that change where data are sparse, which is exactly the **cluster assumption** of ch. 4.

### 3.4 Manifold learning with Laplacian eigenmaps

To embed the nodes in $\mathbb{R}^q$ so that neighbours stay close, minimize the weighted spread of the embedding $y_1, \dots, y_n \in \mathbb{R}^q$, under a normalization that excludes collapse.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Laplacian eigenmaps (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003)]{.tag} Let $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times q}$ have rows $y_i$. The problem
$$
\min_{Y}\ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} w_{ij}\, \|y_i - y_j\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad Y^\top D Y = I_q,\ \ Y^\top D \mathbf{1} = 0
$$
is solved by the generalized eigenvectors $u_2, \dots, u_{q+1}$ of $L u = \lambda D u$, and its value is $\lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_{q+1}$.

::: proof
The objective equals $\mathrm{tr}(Y^\top L Y)$ by Proposition 1.3 applied to each column. With $Z = D^{1/2} Y$, it becomes $\mathrm{tr}(Z^\top L_{\mathrm{sym}} Z)$ under $Z^\top Z = I_q$ and $Z \perp D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$.

The vector $D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$ is the first eigenvector of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$. The Ky Fan part of Theorem 0.1, applied on its orthogonal complement, gives the next $q$ eigenvectors. Returning to $Y = D^{-1/2} Z$ gives generalized eigenvectors (Proposition 1.3). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Laplacian eigenmaps belong to a family of spectral embeddings. Isomap (Tenenbaum, de Silva and Langford, 2000) preserves graph geodesic distances. Locally linear embedding (Roweis and Saul, 2000) preserves local linear reconstructions. Diffusion maps (Coifman and Lafon, 2006) give a distance between nodes from powers of the random walk; ch. 10.2 derives them.

The code builds a 10-NN graph on 1500 noisy points of a Swiss roll, a two-dimensional sheet rolled up in $\mathbb{R}^3$. It compares the first eigenmap coordinate with the position $t$ along the roll, then denoises $\sin t$ in the Laplacian basis.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import diags
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import laplacian, connected_components
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.datasets import make_swiss_roll
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X, t = make_swiss_roll(n_samples=1500, noise=0.1, random_state=0)   # t = position along the roll
W = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=10, include_self=False)
W = W.maximum(W.T)                                    # symmetric 10-NN graph ("or" rule)
print("connected components:", connected_components(W)[0])
L = laplacian(W).astype(float)
D = diags(np.asarray(W.sum(axis=1)).ravel())

# Laplacian eigenmaps: smallest solutions of L u = lambda D u (shift-invert near 0)
vals, vecs = eigsh(L, k=3, M=D, sigma=-1e-3, which="LM")
emb = vecs[:, np.argsort(vals)[1]]                    # first non-constant coordinate
print("|Spearman(t, eigenmap)| =", round(abs(spearmanr(t, emb)[0]), 3))
print("|Spearman(t, PCA)|      =", round(abs(spearmanr(t, PCA(1).fit_transform(X)[:, 0])[0]), 3))

# eigenvectors of L as a nonparametric basis: denoise a smooth function of t
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = np.sin(t)
y = f + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=t.size)                 # noise level sigma = 0.5
vals, U = eigsh(L, k=60, sigma=-1e-3, which="LM")
U = U[:, np.argsort(vals)]
for m in [2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60]:
    fhat = U[:, :m] @ (U[:, :m].T @ y)                # projection on the first m eigenvectors
    print(f"m = {m:2d}: RMSE = {np.sqrt(np.mean((fhat - f) ** 2)):.3f}")
```

The first eigenmap coordinate orders the points along the roll almost perfectly: its rank correlation with $t$ is 0.999, against 0.213 for the first principal component, which only sees the ambient coordinates.

The projection estimator shows the bias–variance trade-off of Proposition 3.2. The RMSE falls from 0.722 ($m = 2$) to 0.074 ($m = 20$), then rises again to 0.100 ($m = 60$), as each extra eigenvector adds variance.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Build a connected, sparse graph: $k$-NN with $k$ of order $\log n$ is a robust default.
-   The first eigenvectors of $L$ form a data-adapted basis; projecting on $m$ of them costs bias $f^\top L f / \lambda_{m+1}$ plus variance $m\sigma^2$.
-   Rescaled graph Laplacians converge to a density-weighted Laplace–Beltrami operator on the data manifold.
-   Laplacian eigenmaps = generalized eigenvectors $2, \dots, q+1$; they unroll curved data that PCA cannot.
:::

## 4. Semi-supervised learning on graphs {#ch4}

Labels are expensive and unlabelled data are cheap: a handful of annotated face images, and thousands of unannotated frames. Semi-supervised learning uses the unlabelled points to shape the predictor. On a graph, the idea is simple: labels should vary little along the edges.

### 4.1 Setting and assumptions

The nodes $1, \dots, n$ are split into $l$ labelled nodes, with labels $y_1, \dots, y_l$, and $u = n - l$ unlabelled ones; typically $l \ll u$. We order the labelled nodes first and split matrices into blocks:
$$
L = \begin{pmatrix} L_{ll} & L_{lu} \\ L_{ul} & L_{uu} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad f = \begin{pmatrix} f_l \\ f_u \end{pmatrix} .
$$

The goal can be **transductive** (label the given unlabelled nodes) or **inductive** (predict at new points). Unlabelled data help only under an assumption linking the inputs to the labels:

-   the **smoothness assumption**: close points in a high-density region have close labels;
-   the **cluster assumption**: the decision boundary goes through low-density regions;
-   the **manifold assumption**: the data lie near a low-dimensional manifold, on which the labels vary smoothly.

The limit of ch. 3.3 shows that the Laplacian energy $f^\top L f$ encodes all three: it penalizes variations where the density is high, along the manifold.

### 4.2 The harmonic function solution

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Harmonic function solution (Zhu, Ghahramani and Lafferty, 2003)]{.tag} The harmonic solution minimizes the Laplacian energy under the constraint that it fits the labels exactly:
$$
f^\star = \arg\min_{f \in \mathbb{R}^n}\ f^\top L f \quad \text{subject to} \quad f_i = y_i \ \ (i \leq l) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Closed form and maximum principle]{.tag} If every connected component of the graph contains a labelled node, then $L_{uu}$ is invertible and the solution is unique:

::: key
[Key formula — the harmonic function solution]{.tag}
$$
f_u^\star = L_{uu}^{-1}\, W_{ul}\, y_l
$$
:::

It is **harmonic** at every unlabelled node, $f^\star_i = \sum_j w_{ij} f^\star_j / d_i$. Hence its values lie between the smallest and the largest label.

::: proof
-   *Invertibility.* If $L_{uu} x = 0$, extend $x$ by zeros on the labelled nodes into $\tilde x$. Then $\tilde x^\top L \tilde x = x^\top L_{uu} x = 0$, so $\tilde x$ is constant on each component (Proposition 1.4), hence zero on every component that contains a labelled node, which is all of them.
-   *Closed form.* The objective is $f_u^\top L_{uu} f_u + 2 f_u^\top L_{ul} y_l + \text{const}$, convex in $f_u$. Its gradient vanishes when $L_{uu} f_u = -L_{ul} y_l = W_{ul} y_l$.
-   *Harmonicity.* Row $i$ of $L f^\star = 0$ on the unlabelled block reads $d_i f^\star_i - \sum_j w_{ij} f^\star_j = 0$.
-   *Maximum principle.* Let $i$ be an unlabelled node where $f^\star$ is largest. As a weighted mean, $f^\star_i$ equals all its neighbours' values. Following a path to a labelled node shows that the maximum is a label. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $C$ classes, solve one problem per class with the one-hot labels as $y_l$, and predict the class of largest value. When the classes are unbalanced, Zhu, Ghahramani and Lafferty (2003) rescale each column to the expected class proportion, a step called **class mass normalization**.

### 4.3 Random walks and electric networks

The harmonic solution has two classical interpretations, which explain why it works and when it fails.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Absorption probabilities]{.tag} Let the labels be in $\{0, 1\}$ and every component contain a labelled node. Run the random walk $P = D^{-1} W$ from node $i$ until it first hits a labelled node. Then
$$
f^\star_i = \mathbb{P}_i\big(\text{the walk is absorbed at a node labelled } 1\big) .
$$

::: proof
Let $h_i$ be this probability. The walk is absorbed almost surely, because from any node a labelled node is reachable in its component. At a labelled node, $h_i = y_i$.

At an unlabelled node, conditioning on the first step gives $h_i = \sum_j P_{ij} h_j$, so $h$ is harmonic there. By the uniqueness in Proposition 4.2, $h = f^\star$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In electrical terms (Doyle and Snell, 1984), put a resistor of conductance $w_{ij}$ on each edge, and hold the nodes labelled 1 at one volt and those labelled 0 at zero volts. Kirchhoff's laws say that the voltage at each free node is the weighted mean of its neighbours' voltages: the voltages are $f^\star$.

A node connected to the 1-labelled nodes by many short paths takes a voltage close to 1, even far from them: labels flow easily within a dense cluster and poorly across a sparse boundary.

### 4.4 Soft constraints and regularization

Hard constraints trust every label. With noisy labels, or to obtain the stability of ch. 5, one replaces them by a penalty and adds a small ridge term.

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Soft harmonic solution]{.tag} Let $C = \mathrm{diag}(c_1, \dots, c_n)$ with $c_i > 0$ on labelled nodes and $c_i = 0$ elsewhere, let $y_i = 0$ on unlabelled nodes, and $Q = L + \gamma I$ with $\gamma \geq 0$. The soft harmonic solution is
$$
f^\star = \arg\min_{f \in \mathbb{R}^n}\ (f - y)^\top C (f - y) + f^\top Q f \ =\ (C + Q)^{-1} C\, y .
$$
:::

The closed form follows by setting the gradient $2C(f - y) + 2Qf$ to zero. As the label weights $c_i \to \infty$ with $\gamma = 0$, the solution tends to the hard harmonic solution.

The ridge term $\gamma > 0$ makes $C + Q$ invertible even without labels in some component, and shrinks predictions towards 0 far from the labels. Zhou and coauthors (2004) use $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ instead, which gives the iteration $F \leftarrow \alpha S F + (1 - \alpha) Y$ with $S = D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}$.

There is a deeper reason to regularize. With a fixed number of labels and more and more unlabelled points in dimension at least 2, the hard harmonic solution becomes almost constant, with spikes at the labels (Nadler, Srebro and Zhou, 2009). Exercise 16 shows it.

### 4.5 Manifold regularization

The harmonic solution is transductive: it gives no value at a new point. Belkin, Niyogi and Sindhwani (2006) combine a kernel model with the graph penalty, to obtain a function defined everywhere.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Representer theorem for manifold regularization]{.tag} Let $K$ be a positive definite kernel with RKHS $\mathcal{H}_K$, $V$ a loss, $\gamma_A, \gamma_I > 0$, and $\hat f = (f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n))$. Every minimizer over $\mathcal{H}_K$ of
$$
\frac{1}{l} \sum_{i=1}^l V\big(y_i, f(x_i)\big) + \gamma_A \|f\|_{K}^2 + \frac{\gamma_I}{n^2}\, \hat f^\top L \hat f
$$
has the form $f = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i K(x_i, \cdot)$: an expansion over **all** points, labelled and unlabelled.

::: proof
Split $f = f_S + f_\perp$, with $f_S$ in the span $S$ of $K(x_1, \cdot), \dots, K(x_n, \cdot)$ and $f_\perp \perp S$.

By the reproducing property, $f(x_i) = \langle f, K(x_i, \cdot)\rangle = f_S(x_i)$ for every $i \leq n$.

The loss and the graph term depend on $f$ only through $\hat f$, so they do not see $f_\perp$. The norm term does: $\|f\|_K^2 = \|f_S\|_K^2 + \|f_\perp\|_K^2$. A minimizer therefore has $f_\perp = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With the squared loss (Laplacian regularized least squares), plug $\hat f = K\alpha$ into the objective. Let $J$ be the diagonal matrix with ones on the labelled nodes, and $Y$ the label vector padded with zeros. Setting the gradient to zero gives, for an invertible Gram matrix $K$,
$$
\alpha = \Big( J K + \gamma_A\, l\, I + \frac{\gamma_I\, l}{n^2}\, L K \Big)^{-1} Y .
$$

With $\gamma_I = 0$ this is kernel ridge regression on the labelled points; with $\gamma_A \to 0$ it approaches a harmonic-type solution. The [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) course develops the RKHS side.

### 4.6 Handwritten digits with 20 labels

The code labels 2 images per class among the 1797 handwritten digits of scikit-learn. It builds a 10-NN graph with Gaussian weights and solves one harmonic problem per class.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import laplacian
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)            # 1797 images of 8 x 8 pixels, 10 classes
X = X / 16.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
lab = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(y == c), 2, replace=False) for c in range(10)])
unl = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), lab)      # 20 labelled, 1777 unlabelled

W = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=10, mode="distance", include_self=False)
W.data = np.exp(-W.data**2 / (2 * np.median(W.data) ** 2))   # Gaussian weights on the 10-NN graph
W = W.maximum(W.T).tocsr()
L = laplacian(W).tocsr()

Y = np.eye(10)[y[lab]]                          # one-hot labels, one harmonic problem per class
F_u = spsolve(L[unl][:, unl].tocsc(), W[unl][:, lab] @ Y)    # L_uu f_u = W_ul y_l
print(f"harmonic solution on the graph : {(F_u.argmax(1) == y[unl]).mean():.3f}")
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X[lab], y[lab])
print(f"logistic regression on 20 images: {(clf.predict(X[unl]) == y[unl]).mean():.3f}")
```

The harmonic solution classifies 91.5 % of the unlabelled images, the supervised logistic regression 80.4 %. The 1777 unlabelled images carry the information: they connect each labelled image to the many images of the same digit written slightly differently.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Harmonic solution: minimize $f^\top L f$ with the labels fixed; $f_u = L_{uu}^{-1} W_{ul} y_l$.
-   It is the probability that a random walk is absorbed at a positive label, and the voltage of an electric network.
-   Soft harmonic: $f = (C + L + \gamma I)^{-1} C y$; regularization handles noisy labels and is needed when unlabelled data abound.
-   Manifold regularization adds $\hat f^\top L \hat f$ to a kernel method; the solution expands over all points.
:::

## 5. Learnability on graphs: transductive learning {#ch5}

The harmonic solution fits the labelled nodes; does it predict the others? Classical learning theory assumes test points drawn from a distribution, but on a graph the test nodes are known in advance. This chapter sets up the transductive framework and proves a generalization bound for the soft harmonic solution, through algorithmic stability.

### 5.1 The transductive setting

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Transductive learning on a graph]{.tag} The graph and the labels $y_1, \dots, y_n$ of all its nodes are fixed. A set $S$ of $l$ nodes is drawn uniformly at random among all subsets of size $l$; its labels are revealed. The learner returns predictions $f_S \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

For a loss $\ell(f_i, y_i)$, the **training** and **test** risks are
$$
\widehat R_S(f) = \frac{1}{l} \sum_{i \in S} \ell(f_i, y_i), \qquad R_U(f) = \frac{1}{u} \sum_{i \notin S} \ell(f_i, y_i), \qquad u = n - l .
$$
:::

This is Vapnik's transduction: the only randomness is the choice of the labelled nodes, a sampling **without replacement**. There is no distribution over new points, and the bound must control the test risk on the $u$ given nodes.

### 5.2 Stability of the soft harmonic solution

Write $S^{ij} = (S \setminus \{i\}) \cup \{j\}$ for $i \in S$ and $j \notin S$: one labelled node is swapped for an unlabelled one.

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Uniform stability under swaps]{.tag} A transductive algorithm is **$\beta$-stable** when, for every $S$, every $i \in S$ and every $j \notin S$,
$$
\big\| f_S - f_{S^{ij}} \big\|_\infty \leq \beta .
$$
:::

We study the soft harmonic solution of Definition 4.4, with equal weights $c / l$ on the labelled nodes:
$$
f_S = \arg\min_{f}\ F_S(f), \qquad F_S(f) = \frac{c}{l} \sum_{i \in S} (f_i - y_i)^2 + f^\top (L + \gamma I) f .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Stability of the soft harmonic solution]{.tag} Assume $|y_i| \leq M$ for all $i$, and $\gamma > 0$. Then $|f_{S,i}| \leq M$ for all nodes, and the algorithm is $\beta$-stable with
$$
\beta = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\, c\, M}{\gamma\, l} .
$$

::: proof
*Step 1, boundedness.* Let $k$ be a node where $f = f_S$ is largest, and $c_k \in \{0, c/l\}$ its label weight. Row $k$ of $(C + L + \gamma I) f = C y$ reads
$$
(c_k + \gamma) f_k + \sum_j w_{kj} (f_k - f_j) = c_k\, y_k .
$$
The sum is non-negative at a maximum, so $(c_k + \gamma) f_k \leq c_k M$ and $f_k \leq M$. The same argument at a minimum gives $f \geq -M$.

*Step 2, strong convexity.* The Hessian of $F_S$ is $2(C + L + \gamma I) \succeq 2\gamma I$. Hence, at its minimizer,
$$
F_S(g) - F_S(f_S) \geq \gamma\, \|g - f_S\|^2 \qquad \text{for all } g .
$$

*Step 3, comparison.* Let $f = f_S$ and $f' = f_{S^{ij}}$. Apply Step 2 to both problems and add:
$$
2\gamma\, \|f - f'\|^2 \leq \big[F_S - F_{S^{ij}}\big](f') - \big[F_S - F_{S^{ij}}\big](f) .
$$
The difference $F_S - F_{S^{ij}}$ keeps only two label terms, $\frac{c}{l}\big[(g_i - y_i)^2 - (g_j - y_j)^2\big]$.

*Step 4, Lipschitz bound.* For $a, b, y \in [-M, M]$, $|(a - y)^2 - (b - y)^2| \leq 4M\, |a - b|$. The right-hand side of Step 3 is therefore at most
$$
\frac{4cM}{l}\big(|f_i - f'_i| + |f_j - f'_j|\big) \leq \frac{4\sqrt{2}\, cM}{l}\, \|f - f'\| .
$$
Dividing by $2\gamma\|f - f'\|$ gives the claim, since $\|f - f'\|_\infty \leq \|f - f'\|$:
$$
\|f - f'\|_\infty \leq \frac{2\sqrt{2}\, cM}{\gamma\, l} .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 5.3 Concentration for sampling without replacement

The labelled set is not a sequence of independent draws, so McDiarmid's inequality does not apply directly. The same martingale argument works with a coupling.

:::: thm
[Lemma 5.4 — Bounded swaps imply concentration]{.tag} Let $S$ be a uniformly random subset of size $l$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Let $h$ be a function of subsets that moves by at most $\kappa$ under any swap:
$$
|h(S) - h(S^{ij})| \leq \kappa \qquad \text{for all } S,\ i \in S,\ j \notin S .
$$
Then, with $m = \min(l, n - l)$ and $t > 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\big( h(S) - \mathbb{E}\, h(S) \geq t \big) \leq \exp\Big( - \frac{2 t^2}{m\, \kappa^2} \Big) .
$$

::: proof
Draw $S$ as the first $l$ entries $Z_1, \dots, Z_l$ of a uniform random ordering, and let $M_k = \mathbb{E}[h(S) \mid Z_1, \dots, Z_k]$, a martingale from $\mathbb{E}\, h$ to $h(S)$.

-   Fix $Z_1, \dots, Z_{k-1}$, and two possible values $a, b$ of $Z_k$. Given $Z_k = a$, the remaining entries are a uniform ordered sample from the nodes not yet drawn.
-   Exchange $a$ and $b$ wherever they appear. This maps the conditional law given $Z_k = a$ onto that given $Z_k = b$.
-   Under this coupling the two sets are equal if $b$ is drawn later, and differ by one swap otherwise. So the two conditional expectations differ by at most $\kappa$.
-   The increment $M_k - M_{k-1}$ therefore lies in an interval of length $\kappa$, and Theorem 0.5 gives the bound with $l$ steps.

The complement of $S$ is a uniform subset of size $n - l$, and $h$ has the same bounded-swap property as a function of the complement. Revealing the complement instead takes $n - l$ steps, hence the minimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 5.4 A transductive generalization bound

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Transductive bound for stable algorithms]{.tag} Let the loss $\ell(\cdot, y)$ be $\Lambda$-Lipschitz and bounded by $B$ on $[-M, M]$. Let the algorithm be $\beta$-stable with predictions in $[-M, M]$. Set
$$
\kappa = 2\Lambda\beta + B\Big(\frac{1}{l} + \frac{1}{u}\Big), \qquad m = \min(l, u) .
$$
Then, for $\delta \in (0, 1)$, with probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the labelled set,

::: key
[Key result — stability gives transductive generalization]{.tag}
$$
R_U(f_S) \ \leq\ \widehat R_S(f_S) + \Lambda \beta + \kappa \sqrt{\frac{m \log(1/\delta)}{2}}
$$
:::

::: proof
Let $\Phi(S) = R_U(f_S) - \widehat R_S(f_S)$.

*Expectation.* Draw $S$, then $I$ uniform in $S$ and $J$ uniform outside $S$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\widehat R_S(f_S) = \mathbb{E}\,\ell(f_{S,I}, y_I), \qquad \mathbb{E}\, R_U(f_S) = \mathbb{E}\,\ell(f_{S,J}, y_J) .
$$

The map $(S, I, J) \mapsto (S^{IJ}, J, I)$ is a bijection of the triples that preserves their uniform law. Hence
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\ell(f_{S,J}, y_J) = \mathbb{E}\,\ell(f_{S^{IJ}, I}, y_I), \qquad \text{so} \qquad \mathbb{E}\,\Phi = \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(f_{S^{IJ}, I}, y_I) - \ell(f_{S,I}, y_I)\big] \leq \Lambda\beta .
$$

*Bounded swaps.* Replacing $S$ by $S^{ij}$ changes every prediction by at most $\beta$, so every loss by at most $\Lambda\beta$.

It also exchanges one term of each average, which costs at most $B/u$ for $R_U$ and $B/l$ for $\widehat R_S$. Hence $|\Phi(S) - \Phi(S^{ij})| \leq \kappa$.

*Concentration.* Lemma 5.4 with $t = \kappa\sqrt{m \log(1/\delta) / 2}$ bounds the probability that $\Phi - \mathbb{E}\Phi \geq t$ by $\delta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the squared loss on $[-M, M]$, $\Lambda = 4M$ and $B = 4M^2$. With Theorem 5.3 the gap between test and training risk is of order
$$
\frac{c\, M^2}{\gamma \sqrt{l}} + \frac{M^2}{\sqrt{l}} \qquad \text{when } u \geq l .
$$

Bounds of this type were proved by Belkin, Matveeva and Niyogi (2004) for graph regularization, and by Cortes, Mohri, Pechyony and Rastogi (2008) for transductive regression. El-Yaniv and Pechyony (2009) develop a transductive Rademacher complexity.

### 5.5 What the bound says

The bound decreases as $1/\sqrt{l}$ and improves as $\gamma$ grows relative to $c$. But strong regularization also shrinks the predictions towards 0. The experiment measures stability on two moons with 100 labels.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import diags, identity
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import laplacian
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph

X, yc = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.1, random_state=0)
y = 2.0 * yc - 1                                    # labels in {-1, +1}, so M = 1
W = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=10, include_self=False)
L = laplacian(W.maximum(W.T)).tocsc()
n, l, c = len(y), 100, 1.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
S = rng.choice(n, l, replace=False)                 # the labelled nodes
U = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), S)

def soft_harmonic(S, gamma):
    """argmin_f (c/l) sum_{i in S} (f_i - y_i)^2 + f^T (L + gamma I) f  (Definition 4.4)."""
    C = np.zeros(n); C[S] = c / l
    return spsolve((diags(C) + L + gamma * identity(n)).tocsc(), C * y)

for gamma in [1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1.0]:
    f = soft_harmonic(S, gamma)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(10):                             # swap a labelled node for an unlabelled one
        i, j = rng.choice(S), rng.choice(U)
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(soft_harmonic(np.append(S[S != i], j), gamma) - f).max())
    beta = 2 * np.sqrt(2) * c / (gamma * l)         # Theorem 5.3 with M = 1
    print(f"gamma = {gamma:5g}: largest change {worst:.4f} <= beta = {beta:7.4g};"
          f" max |f| = {np.abs(f).max():.3f}, test sign error = {np.mean(np.sign(f[U]) != y[U]):.3f}")
```

| $\gamma$ | largest observed change | $\beta$ (Theorem 5.3) | $\max_i \lvert f_i \rvert$ | test sign error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.001 | 0.0157 | 28.3 | 0.274 | 0.341 |
| 0.01 | 0.0058 | 2.83 | 0.103 | 0.063 |
| 0.1 | 0.0022 | 0.283 | 0.017 | 0.002 |
| 1 | 0.0012 | 0.0283 | 0.003 | 0.001 |

Three lessons follow.

-   The theorem holds with a large margin: the worst case is far from a typical swap on a well-connected graph.
-   Larger $\gamma$ makes the solution more stable, and here also more accurate in sign. With $\gamma = 0.001$ the label term is too weak and the solution nearly flat.
-   Stability is bought with shrinkage: $\max|f|$ falls to $0.003$. The squared loss then stays close to 1 on both sets, while the classification by sign is excellent; margin-based losses suit this regime better (Exercise 11).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Transduction: fixed nodes, random labelled subset drawn without replacement, test risk on the given unlabelled nodes.
-   The soft harmonic solution with ridge $\gamma$ and label weight $c/l$ is $2\sqrt{2}\,cM/(\gamma l)$-stable, by strong convexity.
-   Bounded swaps give concentration without replacement, through a coupled martingale.
-   Stability plus concentration: test risk $\leq$ training risk $+\ O\big(1/(\gamma\sqrt{l})\big)$; regularization trades stability against shrinkage.
:::

## 6. Adaptive online learning with graphs {#ch6}

In many applications the data arrive one at a time and a prediction is needed at once: a camera that must name the person in front of it, a network whose nodes are queried in an arbitrary order. This chapter studies two online problems on graphs. The first predicts the labels of a fixed graph with a perceptron; the second learns from a stream of points with bounded memory.

### 6.1 Online prediction of a graph labelling

The graph is fixed and connected, with an unknown labelling $y \in \{-1, +1\}^n$. At each round $t = 1, 2, \dots$ a node $i_t$ is chosen, possibly by an adversary; the learner predicts $\hat y_t$, then sees $y_{i_t}$. The goal is to make few **mistakes**.

No algorithm can do well on every labelling, so the bound must depend on the labelling. The natural complexity is the **cut size**, the weight of the edges whose ends disagree:
$$
\Phi(y) = \sum_{i < j:\ y_i \neq y_j} w_{ij} = \frac{1}{4}\, y^\top L y .
$$

### 6.2 The graph perceptron

The perceptron runs in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space; on a graph the right space comes from the Laplacian.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.1 — The Laplacian RKHS]{.tag} Let the graph be connected and $M = L + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top / n^2$. Then $M$ is positive definite, $\langle f, g \rangle = f^\top M g$ is an inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the reproducing kernel is
$$
K = M^{-1} = L^{+} + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top, \qquad f_i = \langle K e_i, f \rangle \ \ \text{for all } f, i .
$$

::: proof
On $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, $M$ acts as $L$, which is positive definite there since $\lambda_2 > 0$. On $\mathbf{1}$, $M \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}/n$.

So $M$ is positive definite. Its inverse is $L^+$ on $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, plus $n$ times the projector $\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top / n$.

Finally $\langle K e_i, f \rangle = e_i^\top K M f = f_i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The diagonal of $K$ is controlled by **effective resistances**. View each edge as a resistor of conductance $w_{ij}$; the effective resistance between $i$ and $j$ is
$$
r(i, j) = (e_i - e_j)^\top L^{+} (e_i - e_j) .
$$
Let $R_G = \max_{i,j} r(i, j)$. On an unweighted graph, $R_G$ is at most the diameter, because a shortest path alone has resistance equal to its length, and adding edges only lowers resistances.

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Kernel perceptron (Novikoff, 1962)]{.tag} The perceptron starts from $w = 0$, predicts $\hat y_t = \mathrm{sign}\big(w(i_t)\big)$, and on a mistake updates $w \leftarrow w + y_{i_t} K e_{i_t}$. If some $g$ satisfies $y_{i_t}\, g(i_t) \geq 1$ for all $t$, the number of mistakes is at most
$$
\|g\|^2\ \max_t K_{i_t i_t} .
$$

::: proof
Let $w_k$ be the hypothesis after $k$ mistakes, and $\kappa = \max_t K_{i_t i_t}$.

-   At a mistake on node $i = i_t$, the reproducing property gives the progress
    $$
    \langle w_{k+1}, g \rangle = \langle w_k, g \rangle + y_i\, g(i) \geq \langle w_k, g \rangle + 1 .
    $$
-   The norm grows slowly, because a mistake means $y_i\, w_k(i) \leq 0$:
    $$
    \|w_{k+1}\|^2 = \|w_k\|^2 + 2 y_i\, w_k(i) + K_{ii} \leq \|w_k\|^2 + \kappa .
    $$
-   After $k$ mistakes, $\langle w_k, g \rangle \geq k$ and $\|w_k\|^2 \leq k\kappa$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $k \leq \sqrt{k\kappa}\, \|g\|$, so $k \leq \kappa \|g\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Mistake bound of the graph perceptron]{.tag} On a connected graph, the perceptron with the kernel of Proposition 6.1 makes at most
$$
\big(4\, \Phi(y) + 1\big)\,\big(R_G + 1\big)
$$
mistakes on any sequence of nodes, in any order, with any number of repetitions.

::: proof
Take $g = y$, which has margin $y_i g(i) = 1$. Its norm satisfies
$$
\|y\|^2 = y^\top L y + \frac{(\mathbf{1}^\top y)^2}{n^2} \leq 4\Phi(y) + 1 .
$$

For the kernel diagonal, $L^+\mathbf{1} = 0$ gives $\sum_j r(i, j) = n L^+_{ii} + \mathrm{tr}\, L^+$ and $\sum_{i,j} r(i, j) = 2n\, \mathrm{tr}\, L^+$. Hence
$$
L^+_{ii} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j r(i, j) - \frac{1}{2n^2}\sum_{j,k} r(j, k) \leq R_G ,
$$
and $K_{ii} = L^+_{ii} + 1 \leq R_G + 1$. Theorem 6.2 concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The bound depends neither on $n$ nor on the order of the nodes: only on the cut and on how well the graph conducts. This is the result of Herbster, Pontil and Wainer (2005), up to the normalization of the kernel. On a long path $R_G$ is large and the bound weak; Herbster and Pontil (2006) discuss remedies.

The code runs the perceptron on a stochastic block model: two communities of 100 nodes, edge probability 0.1 inside and 0.005 across.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx

G = nx.stochastic_block_model([100, 100], [[0.10, 0.005], [0.005, 0.10]], seed=1)
n = G.number_of_nodes()
y = np.array([1.0 if G.nodes[v]["block"] == 0 else -1.0 for v in G])
L = nx.laplacian_matrix(G).toarray().astype(float)
K = np.linalg.inv(L + np.ones((n, n)) / n**2)       # kernel L^+ + 1 1^T (Proposition 6.1)
Lp = K - 1.0                                         # pseudo-inverse L^+
r = np.diag(Lp)[:, None] + np.diag(Lp)[None, :] - 2 * Lp   # effective resistances
cut = sum(y[a] != y[b] for a, b in G.edges())
print(f"cut size {cut}, R_G = {r.max():.3f}, bound (4 cut + 1)(R_G + 1) = {(4 * cut + 1) * (r.max() + 1):.0f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
alpha, mistakes = np.zeros(n), 0                     # perceptron in dual form: w = K alpha
for epoch in range(3):
    for t in rng.permutation(n):                     # nodes arrive in random order
        pred = 1.0 if K[t] @ alpha >= 0 else -1.0
        if pred != y[t]:
            alpha[t] += y[t]
            mistakes += 1
    print(f"after pass {epoch + 1}: {mistakes} mistakes in total")
```

The labelling cuts 49 edges and $R_G = 0.461$, so the bound is 288 mistakes. The perceptron makes 4, all in the first pass, and none afterwards.

### 6.3 Online semi-supervised learning with bounded memory

Now the graph itself grows. Points $x_1, x_2, \dots$ arrive in a stream, a few of them labelled, and at time $t$ the learner must label $x_t$. Solving the harmonic problem on all $t$ points seen so far costs at least linear time in $t$ per step, and the memory grows without bound.

The remedy of Valko, Kveton, Huang and Ting (2010) is to **quantize**: keep at most $k$ centres $z_1, \dots, z_k$, each with the number $v_j$ of points it stands for. Replacing every point by its centre gives a graph on the centres with weights $v_i v_j\, w(z_i, z_j)$. For functions constant on each cell, its Laplacian quadratic form is that of the replaced full graph.

How much does the solution change when the graph is perturbed? The next proposition answers, and serves again in ch. 7.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Perturbation of the soft harmonic solution]{.tag} Let $L$ and $L'$ be two Laplacians on the same nodes and $\gamma > 0$.

Let $f$ and $f'$ be the soft harmonic solutions (Definition 4.4) computed with $L$ and with $L'$. Then
$$
\|f - f'\| \leq \frac{\|L - L'\|}{\gamma}\, \|f'\| .
$$

::: proof
Subtracting the two linear systems gives $(C + L + \gamma I)(f - f') = (L' - L) f'$. The matrix on the left is at least $\gamma I$ in the Loewner order, so its inverse has norm at most $1/\gamma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If the similarity $w(x, x')$ is $\Lambda_w$-Lipschitz in each argument, moving every point by at most $R$ to its centre changes each weight by at most $2\Lambda_w R$. By Gershgorin's theorem, the Laplacian then changes by at most $4 n \Lambda_w R$ in operator norm. The quantization error vanishes with the distortion $R$ of the quantizer.

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.5 — Online harmonic solution on a quantized graph]{.tag} Parameters: a budget $k$, a similarity, a regularization $\gamma$. Keep the labelled points apart.

1.  When $x_t$ arrives, build the graph on the labelled points, the current centres (with their multiplicities) and $x_t$.
2.  Solve the regularized harmonic problem on this graph of at most $l + k + 1$ nodes, and predict the label of $x_t$.
3.  Add $x_t$ to the quantizer. If more than $k$ centres exist, merge centres, for instance by the doubling rule of the incremental $k$-centre algorithm of Charikar, Chekuri, Feder and Motwani (1997), which keeps a constant-factor approximation of the best $k$-centre radius.
:::

Each step costs a solve on $l + k + 1$ nodes, independent of $t$. Valko and coauthors bound the online error by three terms: a transductive generalization term (ch. 5), an online-learning term, and a quantization term that decreases with the distortion.

### 6.4 The online face recognizer

The official description cites an online face recognizer among the applications of the practical sessions. A camera produces frames, a detector crops the faces, and each face becomes a vector of low-resolution pixels. The user labels a handful of faces per person; the system then names everyone it sees, in real time. With Algorithm 6.5, the unlabelled frames teach the graph how each face varies with pose and lighting, in constant memory.

The code runs the pipeline on the 8 × 8 digit images of scikit-learn, a stand-in for faces since no face data set ships with the library. Two images per class are labelled and the other 1777 arrive in random order. The quantizer merges the two closest centres whenever there are more than 100.

```python
import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")   # one BLAS thread is fastest at these sizes
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X = X / 16.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
order = rng.permutation(len(y)); X, y = X[order], y[order]       # a random stream of images
lab = np.concatenate([np.flatnonzero(y == c)[:2] for c in range(10)])   # 2 labelled per class
stream = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), lab)
Yl, nl, k_nn, gamma, k_max = np.eye(10)[y[lab]], len(lab), 8, 1e-3, 100

def harmonic(P):
    """Regularized harmonic solution on a k-NN graph; the first nl rows of P are labelled."""
    sq = (P**2).sum(1)
    D2 = np.maximum(sq[:, None] + sq[None] - 2 * P @ P.T, 0); np.fill_diagonal(D2, np.inf)
    nn = np.argpartition(D2, k_nn, axis=1)[:, :k_nn]
    rows = np.repeat(np.arange(len(P)), k_nn)
    d2 = D2[rows, nn.ravel()]
    W = np.zeros_like(D2); W[rows, nn.ravel()] = np.exp(-d2 / np.median(d2))
    W = np.maximum(W, W.T)
    L = np.diag(W.sum(1)) - W
    return np.linalg.solve(L[nl:, nl:] + gamma * np.eye(len(P) - nl), W[nl:, :nl] @ Yl)

Z, v, hits = np.empty((0, 64)), np.empty(0), []
for i in stream:
    F = harmonic(np.vstack([X[lab], Z, X[i]]))          # graph on labelled + centres + new image
    hits.append(F[-1].argmax() == y[i])                  # predict, then learn
    Z, v = np.vstack([Z, X[i]]), np.append(v, 1.0)
    if len(Z) > k_max:                                   # merge the two closest centres
        sq = (Z**2).sum(1); D2 = sq[:, None] + sq[None] - 2 * Z @ Z.T
        np.fill_diagonal(D2, np.inf)
        a, b = np.unravel_index(D2.argmin(), D2.shape)
        Z[a] = (v[a] * Z[a] + v[b] * Z[b]) / (v[a] + v[b]); v[a] += v[b]
        Z, v = np.delete(Z, b, 0), np.delete(v, b)
hits = np.array(hits)
print(f"online, {k_max} centres: accuracy {hits.mean():.3f}"
      f" (first 300 images {hits[:300].mean():.3f}, last 300 {hits[-300:].mean():.3f})")
F = harmonic(np.vstack([X[lab], X[stream]]))             # batch: all images at once
print(f"batch, all {len(stream)} images: accuracy {(F.argmax(1) == y[stream]).mean():.3f}")
```

The online learner labels 75.1 % of the stream correctly with 100 centres in memory. The batch harmonic solution, which sees all 1777 images at once with the same labels and graph rule, reaches 79.8 %: the gap is the price of constant memory and of predicting before seeing the future.

The code drops the multiplicities, which are designed for a fully connected graph rather than a $k$-NN graph; Exercise 14 compares the two variants. With two labels per class the accuracy also depends on which images are labelled: ch. 4.6 drew another set and reached 91.5 % in batch.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   The kernel $K = L^+ + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ turns the perceptron into a graph learner; its mistakes are at most $(4\Phi(y) + 1)(R_G + 1)$, whatever the order of the nodes.
-   Effective resistances measure how well the graph conducts information; they bound the kernel diagonal.
-   On a stream, quantize: keep $k$ centres with multiplicities and solve on $O(l + k)$ nodes per step.
-   The soft harmonic solution moves by at most $\|L - L'\|\, \|f'\| / \gamma$ when the graph is perturbed.
:::
